newsitem.title: SPAIN: NATO backs Plavsic in dispute with Karadzic.
newsitem.headline: NATO backs Plavsic in dispute with Karadzic.

text.p: NATO leaders, voicing deep concern over an alleged anti-democratic climate and abuses of police power, on Tuesday strongly backed Bosnian Serb leader Biljana Plavsic in her battle with hardliners in the Bosnian Serb republic.

"The democratic process is being distorted in order to block the constitutional decisions of the elected president of Republika Srpska which must be respected," they said in a statement issued at a NATO enlargement summit in Madrid.

The statement called on hardliners allied to indicted war criminal and ex-Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic to resolve their differences peacefully, warning they faced even greater isolation from the international community if not.
"We will not tolerate any recourse to force or violence, or the unauthorised deployment of military or paramilitary force," the statement warned.

Opponents of Plavsic have scoffed at international warnings they were flouting the law by refusing to accept a presidential decision to dissolve parliament, threatening the prospect of two rival governments in the Bosnian Serb Republic.
The United States and European governments say Plavsic acted in line with the constitution last week when she dissolved the Bosnian Serb assembly and called new elections for September 1.

The statement warned the hardliners they were acting in defiance of the Dayton peace accords, which a 35,000-strong NATO-led force is policing, and called on them to resolve their differences peacefully and through dialogue.
"We demand that police in Republika Srpska halt acts of intimidation and comply fully with all provisions of the peace agreement," the statement said.

NATO countries, which have been criticised for failing to take action to detain Karadzic, again called on the leaders of the region to fulfill their obligation to hand over all indicted war criminals to the international tribunal in The Hague.

But the statement avoided any suggestion NATO leaders might be prepared to change the mission's mandate to go after Karadzic despite recent hints the United States and its allies were hardening their stance.
"Now the issue is more 'Can they afford not to act?'," one official said, adding both the United States and the Europeans were determined to pull out their forces as planned next summer.
"Time is running out to make the (Dayton) peace accords work and with Karadzic there they will not. That is the dilemma," the official said.
NATO leaders also agreed to order a study on ways to try to bring more stability to the turbulent Balkan area in general.

Analysts say NATO states, arguing that the alliance's eastwards expansion into Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, will extend stability, do not want to be accused of failing to have any policy for the continent's most unstable area.
Albania is in turmoil amid constant fears unrest could spread to the Serb province of Kosovo where ethnic Albanians heavily outnumber Serb nationalists.

NATO officials said alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana had held urgent telephone talks with Carlos Westendorp, a fellow Spaniard and the international High Representative to Bosnia, on Tuesday morning.
